title: Reform preferences of key actors in the UNFCCC process
description: COP meetings have faced criticism and calls for reform, yet evidence on reform choices remains limited. Here a survey of COP participants reveals broad support for enhancing transparency and implementation, while proposals to change consensus rules or the COP presidency are less favoured.

paragraphs.text: Calls to reform the United Nations Conferences of the Parties (COPs) climate negotiations have intensified, yet systematic empirical evidence on the reform preferences of key participants remains limited. Here, using a conjoint survey experiment involving state and non-state elite respondents comparing pairs of hypothetical reform proposals, we find broad support for reforms that enhance transparency and provide a stronger implementation focus to drive climate action. We see that non-state actors are more supportive of reforms that limit fossil fuel company participation and expand opportunities for observer engagement. Furthermore, most other institutional reform proposals do not draw substantial support. These results identify two possible reform pathways: to strengthen transparency and accountability, or to reorient COPs towards strengthening the implementation of existing commitments. More contested reforms, including changes to the consensus rule, the COP presidency and stakeholder representation, are less likely to succeed.

As new temperature records are broken and the global carbon budget is fast shrinking1, the multilateral process that in 2015 delivered the Paris Agreement has come under heavy criticism. The United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) has held annual Conferences of the Parties (COPs) for over three decades as the key multilateral forum to address climate change. While considerable progress has been made over the years, the climate crisis is outpacing the multilateral response. Calls for reforming the UNFCCC process broadly, and the COPs more specifically, have thus proliferated in recent years and a range of distinct reform options have been proposed by scholars2,3,4,5,6,7 and by practitioners and diplomats inside the negotiations process8. Such options include changes to decision-making procedures, the roles of observers, COP presidency selection and changes in the focus of negotiations9. Yet, empirical data on which options are widely supported by key actors remain limited.

In this Article, we present a systematic assessment of the reform preferences of COP participants. We conducted an original, fully randomized conjoint survey experiment targeting two main groups at COP meetings: state representatives—particularly those designated as national focal points in the UNFCCC, heads of delegation and other key officials who are central to a state’s engagement with the UNFCCC—and non-state actors, whose roles include influencing state representatives, providing expertise and mobilizing public pressure. The survey asked these actors to evaluate a set of reform proposals that were derived from ongoing policy debates on UNFCCC reform10,11 as well as recent academic contributions9,12. For the purposes of the experiment, we condensed these proposals and reformulated them in clear, accessible language to ensure comparability across respondents (Table 1).

We draw on two analytical perspectives to guide our expectations. First, institutional theory suggests that states embedded in consensus-based multilateral settings tend to favour the status quo or incremental change, as decision rules and agenda control generate institutional conservatism13. Second, research on non-state actor participation in global governance highlights how legitimacy, procedural fairness and access shape the preferences of civil society and other observers, who typically advocate for more open deliberation and stronger implementation mechanisms14,15,16,17. Together, these perspectives lead us to expect systematic preference differences between state and non-state actors, with the latter more supportive of reforms that empower observers, constrain vested interests, and strengthen accountability.

Our study makes two key contributions. Empirically, it provides new experimental evidence of reform preferences among COP participants, identifying where support is broad enough to potentially overcome the consensus threshold. Methodologically, it introduces conjoint survey experimentation to the study of UNFCCC reform—an approach capable of generating causally identified estimates of how actors evaluate competing institutional options, something qualitative approaches alone cannot provide. By surveying both state representatives and non-state actors, we also map points of convergence and divergence among the elites who shape COP negotiations.

The preregistered forced-choice conjoint survey experiment conducted among COP29 participants yielded 151 completed responses, including 63 state representatives (14.0% response rate) and 88 non-state actors (27.8% response rate). State representatives in our sample are mainly designated national focal points in the UNFCCC, typically high-level officials from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs or Environment, such as ambassadors, deputy ministers or head of delegation. They have central knowledge of their country’s official stance but may not always be the lead negotiators18. Non-state representatives in our sample are influential observers from organizations with sizeable delegations at the COP from each constituency group and therefore among the most active and visible participants. These non-state actors typically seek to influence negotiations by providing expertise, shaping public narratives and mobilizing pressure on state negotiators19,20. While our sample is not fully representative of all state representatives or non-state actors—reflecting the inherent challenges of obtaining responses from elite participants—it nevertheless captures state representatives from a wide range of geographic regions. The response rate and total number of respondents compare well with those achieved in other prominent elite survey studies in international relations21,22,23,24.

Respondents were drawn from a broad range of geographic regions (Fig. 1; see also Extended Data Tables 1 and 2 and Supplementary Fig. 1). While there is an overrepresentation of European non-state actors (primarily non-governmental organizations (NGOs)) and slight underrepresentation from the Asia-Pacific region, the sample is otherwise relatively balanced across regions (see the Methods for further details).

Each respondent completed six forced-choice tasks. In each task, respondents saw two complete reform proposals and selected the one they preferred. Each proposal was created by randomly drawing one level from each attribute listed in Table 1. The six rows in Table 1 therefore show the building blocks of the proposals. The full survey instrument is reproduced in the Supplementary Information (Item A), including the introductory instructions and the exact question used for each choice: “Which proposal do you prefer, Proposal 1 or Proposal 2?”. An example of the choice screen shown to respondents is provided in Supplementary Fig. 6.

This procedure produced 1,812 profile evaluations: 151 respondents completed six tasks, with two proposals per task. These evaluations form the basis for all average marginal component effects (AMCEs) and marginal means (MMs) reported below. Randomizing both attribute levels and attribute order helps to reduce potential bias from order effects or attribute framing25.

This design enables us to assess which reform directions stakeholders prioritize across key institutional dimensions. The six attributes were selected to span the main institutional levers of COP reform identified in both academic scholarship2,6,9,12 and practitioner proposals8,10,11: the leadership structure of COPs (presidency), collective decision rules, the composition of participants, the role of observers, accountability for national commitments, and the balance between negotiation and implementation. Other dimensions—such as the frequency of COPs or the mandate of the UNFCCC Secretariat—were considered but excluded to keep the cognitive burden manageable.

The COP presidency attribute contrasts the current regional rotation with proposals to prioritize either climate-leading or vulnerable countries. Decision-making varies between the existing consensus rule and reforms introducing majority voting, either for all decisions or only for non-key issues. Stakeholder representation compares the status quo of open participation with reforms that either limit fossil-fuel company involvement or strengthen support for underrepresented groups. The role of observers ranges from today’s limited interaction with negotiators to options expanding or reducing engagement. Transparency and accountability contrast basic reporting with reforms aimed at enhancing transparency or implementing comprehensive tracking of national climate actions. Finally, the implementation attribute ranges from the status quo emphasis on negotiation to proposals shifting towards a balanced approach or a stronger focus on implementing climate solutions. The exact wording of each attribute and attribute level is presented in Table 1, although the status quo (SQ) labels were not shown to respondents.

sections.heading: Relative support for COP reform proposals

paragraphs.text: Our results show how actors perceive the COP process and which reforms they are more likely to find acceptable. This Article therefore provides an evidence base for identifying politically feasible change. In the pooled sample, support varies substantially across reform proposals (Fig. 2). Each estimate (AMCE) reflects how much more or less likely respondents were to select a reform proposal when it contained a specific attribute level, compared to the status quo for that attribute. An estimate of +0.10, for instance, means a proposal containing that feature was chosen about 10 percentage points more often than one with the status quo option, all else equal; an estimate of –0.10 means it was chosen 10 percentage points less often. Estimates at zero indicate indifference relative to the status quo.
Fig. 2: Support for reform proposals at COP meetings.

Effects are estimated relative to the status quo (SQ) category for each attribute, as defined in Table 1. Squares represent AMCE estimates for the full sample (N = 151 respondents; 1,812 profile evaluations), circles represent AMCE estimates for state representatives (n = 63 respondents), and triangles represent AMCE estimates for non-state actors (n = 88 respondents). Horizontal bars indicate 95% CIs. Standard errors are clustered by respondent to account for repeated choices within individuals. Positive values indicate that an attribute level increases the probability that a proposal is selected relative to the status quo, whereas negative values indicate reduced support. The unit of analysis is the profile evaluation. The complete statistical results corresponding to Fig. 2 are reported in Supplementary Table 1.

We find substantial variation in participants’ views depending on the type of COP reform (Fig. 2). Three findings stand out. First, participants support a more hybrid approach to decision-making—maintaining consensus for key issues while allowing majority voting on less critical ones—over the current all-consensus status quo. Second, and most strongly, respondents favour transparency and accountability reforms: both enhanced reporting of national actions and comprehensive tracking of all climate commitments receive positive estimates, with the more ambitious tracking option drawing somewhat stronger support. Third, participants prefer shifting COPs towards implementation, or at least balancing negotiation and implementation, rather than the current emphasis on negotiation.

By contrast, reforms to the COP presidency—whether prioritizing climate-leading or vulnerable countries over the current regional rotation—draw close to zero support. Changes to stakeholder representation also attract neither strong support nor opposition in the pooled sample; both limiting fossil-fuel participation and increasing support for the underrepresented yield modest positive but non-statistical estimates. On the role of observers, increasing interactions between observers and negotiators attracts modest positive support, while reducing interactions is viewed negatively. Taken together, the pooled results indicate that transparency and implementation reforms enjoy the clearest areas of shared support, while presidency and representation reforms generate limited momentum. We now examine whether these patterns differ between state and non-state actors.

sections.heading: Differences between state representatives and non-state actors

paragraphs.text: Preferences differ in several respects between state representatives and non-state actors (Fig. 2). In our sample, state representatives show broad indifference towards reforms related to the COP presidency, decision-making rules, representation and observer participation. Their preferences are more pronounced, however, when it comes to transparency and implementation. For example, state representatives prefer proposals that introduce comprehensive tracking of all climate actions (AMCE 0.131, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.038 to 0.223, or by 13 percentage points) and for reforms that enhance the transparency of national climate actions (AMCE 0.113, 95% CI 0.038 to 0.189), relative to the status quo.

Consistent with our expectations, non-state actors are more supportive of reforms that increase transparency and empower marginalized groups. Specifically, non-state actors express support for proposals to enhance transparency of national climate actions (AMCE 0.146, 95% CI 0.072 to 0.220) and to implement comprehensive tracking of all climate actions (AMCE 0.117, 95% CI 0.044 to 0.190), relative to the status quo. They also express a preference for reforms that would limit the participation of fossil fuel companies and associated interests (AMCE 0.093, 95% CI 0.007 to 0.178) and for proposals to increase interactions between observers and negotiators (AMCE 0.114, 95% CI 0.033 to 0.196), relative to the respective baseline categories. Furthermore, in line with our expectations, non-state actors show statistically significant opposition to proposals that would reduce interactions between observers and negotiators by 8 percentage points (AMCE −0.081, 95% CI −0.160 to −0.002), whereas state representatives display indifference on this issue. Put simply, non-state actors showed clearer and more consistent preferences, especially for reforms that empower observers and constrain fossil fuel interests.

Taken together, the results suggest that the main differences between state representatives and non-state actors concern observer participation and the role of fossil fuel interests (Fig. 2). On transparency and implementation, however, the two groups display more similar preferences, with both expressing support for reforms that strengthen tracking and accountability in the COP process.

sections.heading: Absolute support for COP reform proposals

paragraphs.text: Reform preferences can be evaluated both relative to the status quo and in absolute terms. AMCEs estimate how reform proposals change the probability of selection relative to existing arrangements (Fig. 2). MMs, by contrast, capture absolute levels of support for each reform option (Fig. 3). This allows an assessment of how strongly each group supports a given option, rather than merely whether it is preferred to the baseline. An MM above 0.5 indicates that a reform option is chosen more often than not; an MM of 0.5 signals indifference; and an MM below 0.5 indicates that the option is disfavoured. MMs are generally preferred for subgroup comparisons because they avoid potentially misleading inferences that can arise when groups differ in their evaluation of the status quo26.

The MMs indicate that participants are largely indifferent to reforms related to COP presidency and decision-making. Differences emerge on representation and the role of observers: non-state actors favour reforms consistent with the pattern in Fig. 2—most visibly increasing observer–negotiator interactions, which receives the highest level of support among all reforms shown in Fig. 3 (MM 0.611, 95% CI 0.565 to 0.657)—and also lean towards limiting fossil fuel participation (MM 0.542, 95% CI 0.491 to 0.592), whereas state representatives are closer to indifferent on these items. At the same time, both groups support transparency reforms, especially comprehensive tracking of all climate actions among state representatives (MM 0.555, 95% CI 0.500 to 0.610), and enhanced transparency of national climate actions among non-state actors (MM 0.559, 95% CI 0.515 to 0.603), as well as a stronger implementation focus. Among state representatives, support is highest for comprehensive tracking (MM 0.555, 95% CI 0.500 to 0.610) and implementation-focused reforms (MMs 0.527, 95% CI 0.475 to 0.580), whereas among non-state actors the strongest support is observed for increased observer–negotiator interactions (MM 0.611, 95% CI 0.565 to 0.657).

When state representatives are divided into global north and global south subgroups, one clear pattern stands out (Extended Data Fig. 1). Representatives from the global south are considerably more supportive of proposals to enhance the participation of underrepresented groups (MM 0.565, 95% CI 0.504 to 0.626) than their counterparts from the global north (MM 0.423, 95% CI 0.347 to 0.498). Preferences regarding transparency and implementation are similar across the two subgroups, suggesting that the main findings are not driven by one single regional group. Among non-state actors, the global north–south comparison shows similarly little regional variation, with both groups supporting greater observer participation, transparency, and implementation-focused reforms (Extended Data Fig. 2).

Together, the results connect the scholarly debate on UNFCCC reform to the evidence base that practitioners and diplomats bring to the negotiating room. First, they identify which reforms may be politically feasible even under consensus rules. Our findings suggest that transparency and implementation reforms enjoy relatively broad acceptance among both state and non-state actors, indicating that these areas may offer the most viable entry points for incremental change. However, consensus rules mean that feasibility depends not only on aggregate support but on the absence of strong veto players. Because UNFCCC decisions typically require unanimity, even widely supported reforms can stall if a few powerful states oppose them. Nevertheless, building broad coalitions enhances legitimacy. It raises the political cost of obstruction by creating normative peer-pressure, making it more costly for veto players to block reforms12,27.

Yet, some reforms within the UNFCCC do not depend on consensus but are in the hands of the political leadership of the Executive Secretary and the Presidency12. For instance, COP30 was named the COP of Implementation by the Brazilian Presidency, who sought to shape the Global Action Agenda to accelerate implementation. The COP30 outcome also included the Global Implementation Accelerator as a voluntary initiative led by the COP Presidencies. This demonstrates that agency of key actors can drive change when there is some demand for new initiatives.

Moving forward with transparency reforms involves balancing competing interests while avoiding undue bureaucratic burdens on states. Although transparency reforms appear politically attractive, they have repeatedly faced resistance from influential states concerned about sovereignty, fairness and exposure of climate finance flows6,13,28. Reforms could therefore be designed to reduce perceived risks, for example by coupling stricter transparency requirements with flexibility and substantial capacity-building support to strengthen countries’ monitoring, evaluation and learning systems. Accordingly, transparency may be positioned as an enabler of national capacities and access to support rather than as a compliance enforcement tool8,29.

Against this backdrop, it is useful to consider what broadly supported reform options could look like in practice. A shift towards implementation may involve stronger follow-up mechanisms, greater emphasis on stocktaking, or expanded technical dialogue. Additional options include regional implementation hubs for tailored assistance, dedicated funding for monitoring and evaluation systems, and linking global stocktake outcomes to targeted capacity-building and finance allocations. Likewise, increased transparency could take the form of clearer reporting and accountability procedures or a stronger focus on monitoring, reporting and verification, although such measures may require additional support for lower-capacity countries9. Importantly, increased transparency does not necessarily conflict with reducing bureaucracy if reporting systems are simplified or streamlined.

Second, the results highlight which reforms are more contested. Limited support for changes to the COP presidency or representation rules suggests that these proposals would require substantial coalition-building to advance. Notably, changing the consensus rule does not emerge as a priority among respondents, in contrast to its prominence in much of the literature—an observation consistent with qualitative research on UNFCCC reform12. By identifying where support is strongest and weakest, the findings clarify which reform pathways are most likely to gain traction within the UNFCCC process.

Resistance to these reforms is not surprising. Presidency rotation reflects the UN’s regional-group balance; participation rules implicate states’ authority over accreditation; and consensus decision-making is widely seen by Parties as safeguarding sovereign equality6,30. Reforming these arrangements therefore carries higher political costs. Any such contested reforms should be pursued with caution, so as not to distract from the more feasible transparency and implementation agenda, where state and non-state actors show broader agreement.

The study advances understanding of preferences for UNFCCC reform and differences across actor groups. One limitation is that focusing on regional groupings prevents differentiation between state actors from distinct party coalitions, limiting insight into power asymmetries in support for specific proposals. Future research could build on these results to examine coalition-building and agency in driving reform. Given ongoing efforts to improve the efficiency of the UNFCCC process8 and the mounting pressures resulting from the withdrawal of the USA, understanding reform preferences among key actors remains important for both researchers and practitioners.

Reform proposals focused on transparency, accountability and implementation command the strongest agreement between state and non-state actors, and should therefore prioritized by the UNFCCC in the near term. Concretely, this could involve strengthening the Enhanced Transparency Framework with flexibility and capacity-building support for lower-capacity countries, improving follow-up and stocktaking mechanisms, and linking the global stocktake more directly to finance and implementation support. By contrast, reforms to the COP presidency, participation rules and consensus-based decision-making remain more contested and are unlikely to move forward without sustained coalition-building. Pushing all such reforms simultaneously risk stalling progress where agreement already exists. Lower-cost avenues, such as presidency-led initiatives and voluntary coalitions, can instead be used to test more contested ideas as political space opens. Overall, the finding point to a two-track strategy that advances transparency and implementation now, while gradually building support for more difficult reforms over time.

Conjoint survey experiments—also referred to as forced-choice designs—are particularly well suited for this study, as they allow us to assess whether institutional reforms matter to COP29 participants25,26. Conjoint experiments are a well-established experimental approach for studying preferences regarding institutional reforms of agreements, policies, and international organizations31,32. We chose this design for two main reasons. First, the forced-choice format generates causally identified estimates of how actors weight competing reform options simultaneously, something that, for instance, open-ended questions cannot provide. In each forced-choice task, respondents were shown two complete reform packages and asked to select the one they preferred. Each package was assembled by independently drawing one level from every attribute listed in Table 1, so that the unit of evaluation was always a composite bundle of six attribute levels. This format forces respondents to reveal trade-off preferences across attributes rather than expressing support for every reform. Second, the fully randomized attribute assignment ensures that any estimated preference effect is not confounded by the order or framing of individual attributes25. We presented the survey to participants as a study on preferences regarding institutional arrangements for COP meetings, deliberately framing the exercise in neutral terms to minimize social desirability pressures and avoid cueing respondents toward either reform or status quo position. The survey consent page explained that participation was voluntary, anonymous, and for academic purposes only.

Our conjoint survey experiment was fielded in several steps. First, we identified samples of state and non-state actors. For state representatives at COP29, we used the official list of national focal points, available on the UNFCCC website, as our initial frame. Most countries had one or two designated focal points, whom we recorded as primary contacts. We then cross-checked these individuals against the comprehensive attendance list for COP29 to confirm their presence (by registration). In addition, we reviewed the full list of state participants at the COP to identify additional relevant officials, including ambassadors, agency directors, heads of delegation and expert advisors. COP29 participation was used as an inclusion criterion to ensure that all sampled state representatives were members of their country’s negotiation team. This strategy also increased the likelihood that state representatives had recent experience with the UNFCCC, enabling more meaningful responses to the institutional reforms featured in the conjoint survey. On average, this approach yielded 2.2 representatives per country, resulting in a final population of 449 state representatives.

For non-state actors, we built on Green’s19 methodology to identify the most influential non-state actors/observers at the COP—defined as those in the top 10th percentile of total delegates sent to the meeting, stratified by actor type. We relied on the list of admitted NGO focal points, also available on the UNFCCC website, to gather contact details for these organizations. In total, we compiled a sample of 317 non-state actors, comprising business and industry NGOs (BINGOs; n = 47), environmental NGOs (ENGOs; n = 143), farmers and agricultural NGOs (Farmers; n = 5), Indigenous Peoples organizations (IPOs; n = 10), local governments and municipal authorities (LGMAs; n = 5), research and independent NGOs (RINGOs; n = 76), trade union NGOs (TUNGOs; n = 6), women and gender constituencies (WGCs; n = 7), youth NGOs (YOUNGOs; n = 15) and intergovernmental organizations (IGOs; n = 3).

In the second stage, we programmed our conjoint survey experiment in Qualtrics and piloted it on-site at COP29 in Baku, Azerbaijan. This pilot study enabled us to assess the cognitive demands on respondents and their comprehension of the conjoint design. Given the practical challenges of recruiting responses from state elites, we focused our efforts on targeting state representatives. The participants were recruited in two ways, First, we approached the country pavilions in the order they were standing from the entrance to the room, and, second, in the corridors leading to the negotiation rooms. The pilot survey was administered via tablet devices. Respondents were given the opportunity to provide feedback after completing the survey, and we deliberately refrained from interfering while surveys were in progress. Due to the tight schedules of state representatives and the limited number of days available during COP29, we received 17 completed surveys from the state representatives, each followed by a brief interview regarding the survey experience. We paid close attention to the concerns raised by respondents after they completed the conjoint survey. Unlike survey experiments with citizen samples, where participation is often incentivized with payment, state elites have fewer incentives and are generally more sensitive to survey length and cognitive burden. As a result, feedback from respondents on-site in Baku led us to make targeted revisions to our preregistered survey (see a full statement on deviations in Supplementary Table 5). While the features of the conjoint design were preserved, we opted to drop the rating task that was included initially, as many respondents found it cumbersome and time-consuming, and noted that it contributed to greater cognitive load. In conjoint studies, rating tasks are frequently included as a robustness check, whereas the forced-choice component is generally regarded as the primary analysis25,26. We also removed several background questions for the same reason. Importantly, on-site follow-up interviews after survey completion increased our confidence that respondents understood the instructions for the conjoint experiment, as well as the specific reform proposals presented. Because the conjoint design features were not changed, the 17 responses were included in the final sample.

In designing our conjoint experiment, we implemented a fully randomized conjoint design, wherein every attribute level was independently drawn at random from its respective set of possible levels. Given our relatively small sample and the anticipated low response rate, we selected six paired reform proposal tasks per respondent, consistent with established recommendations on task numbers for conjoint studies. To minimize the risk of priming respondents toward status quo bias and, perhaps more importantly, to mitigate potential social desirability bias—particularly among state respondents—we deliberately chose not to label baseline categories as the ‘status quo’. This approach increases our confidence that respondents express their genuine preferences regarding institutional reforms of COP meetings, rather than defaulting to or concealing support for the existing institutional arrangements. Furthermore, recognizing the sensitive context of a survey on UNFCCC reforms—where state representatives might perceive the expression of preferences as potentially reflecting their country’s negotiation stance—we omitted any questions about respondents’ country of origin. Instead, we asked about their broader geographical region to assess whether our sample included state representatives from different parts of the world and to enable additional analyses based on regional representation.

The six attributes were selected to reflect the core institutional dimensions of UNFCCC reform currently debated in both academic literature and practitioner discussions2,8,10,11,12. We use these sources to identify the main levers through which the COP process could be reformed: who leads it, how decisions are made, who participates, what role observers play, how accountable the process is, and whether it prioritizes negotiation or implementation. Other potential attributes—such as the frequency of COPs or the role of the UNFCCC Secretariat—were considered but excluded to keep the task cognitively manageable for elite respondents. To reduce framing bias, we kept attribute level descriptions neutral and descriptive, avoided normatively loaded language and pilot-tested the survey on-site at COP29 to verify that respondents understood the options as intended.

We presented the survey to participants as a study on preferences regarding institutional arrangements for COP meetings, without framing it in terms reform or status quo. More specifically, after agreeing to participate in the survey, respondents answered three background questions. They were asked which group they belonged to, which region they were from and how many COP meetings they had previously attended, followed by the introductory text to the conjoint survey experiment (see Supplementary Information Item A for the full questionnaire).

Respondents then proceeded to the conjoint experiment. For each task, they were asked to carefully review the two proposals and then answer the following question: “Which proposal do you prefer, Proposal 1 or Proposal 2? Please choose one proposal.” An example of the choice screen shown to respondents is provided in Supplementary Fig. 6. Following this introduction, we then presented respondents with the conjoint experiment asking them to carefully review the proposals for each task, and then asked the question: “Which proposal do you prefer (Proposal 1or Proposal 2)? Please choose one proposal.”

Following the pilot study, we distributed an anonymous survey link to our full sample of respondents, with data collection completed on 5 June 2025. A total of 215 participants opened the survey, of whom 151 completed the full set of conjoint tasks; the remaining 64 partially completed responses were not included in the analysis. The 151 completed responses, which constitute the final analytic sample used throughout the Article, correspond to an overall response rate of 19.7%. Among state representatives, the response rate was 14.0%, whereas among non-state actors it was 27.8%. While our sample size is relatively small and cannot claim to be fully representative of all state representatives or non-state actors, this limitation reflects the well-known challenges of conducting elite surveys in international politics. Access to policymakers and negotiators is inherently constrained, and response rates are typically low in this type of research. Although respondents were drawn from all major world regions, response rates were higher in Europe and Africa, and somewhat lower in the Americas and the Asia-Pacific region (Extended Data Table 2). If individuals who chose not to participate systematically differ in their reform preferences from those who did respond, this could bias the estimated levels of support for some reform proposals. The results should be interpreted with the caveat that reform support may be more reflective of the perspectives of highly engaged or more accessible delegates. However, some concerns are partly mitigated because the heterogeneous treatment effect analyses by geography reveal that reform preferences are consistent across regions, suggesting that even if non-response varies by region, it is unlikely to meaningfully change the pattern of estimated AMCEs or MMs. Moreover, our survey includes state representatives from a diverse set of geographic regions and achieves response rates comparable to, or higher than, those reported in other elite survey studies (for example, refs. 21,22). Importantly, the design of the conjoint experiment ensures that even with a modest number of respondents, we are able to extract systematic evidence on how actors evaluate competing reform options. The results should therefore be interpreted as providing experimental evidence on reform preferences among COP participants, rather than as definitive population-level estimates.

The final sample includes a relatively balanced distribution of respondents across world regions. However, non-state actor responses were not evenly distributed across regions or actor groups. Most respondents were based in Europe (Supplementary Fig. 1), and a majority self-identified as NGO or ENGO representatives (Extended Data Table 1 and Supplementary Fig. 2).This skew is consistent with our sampling strategy, which prioritized the most influential non-state actors, which usually originate from the global north.

Additional information is provided in the Supplementary Information. Supplementary Fig. 5 presents an additional subgroup analysis by respondents’ prior COP experience, with complete statistical results reported in Supplementary Table 4. Deviations from the preregistered analysis plan are summarized in Supplementary Table 5, and the study preregistration is reproduced in Supplementary Information Item B.

To assess support for reform proposals, we employed a choice-based conjoint experiment, which enables causal estimation of the AMCEs25. In all AMCE models, standard errors are clustered at the respondent level to account for the non-independence of choices within respondents, who each completed 6 paired tasks (yielding 12 total choices per respondent). For subgroup analyses, we follow Leeper et al.26 and estimate MMs instead of AMCEs. This approach is recommended because subgroups may differ in their baseline assessment of specific attribute levels, such as the status quo proposal in our design, making direct comparison of AMCEs across groups potentially misleading. MMs represent the absolute probability that a given profile or attribute level is selected, averaging over the distribution of all other attributes26, and thus provide a more interpretable measure of support within subgroups.

Three features of the design support the reliability and internal validity of our estimates. First, because every attribute level was independently and fully randomized within each profile, the estimated AMCEs and MMs are identified without strong parametric assumptions and are not confounded by the order or framing of other attributes25. To assess the quality of randomization, Supplementary Figs. 3 and 4 report feature frequency diagnostics and balance tests, respectively. Second, standard errors are clustered at the respondent level to account for the non-independence of each respondent’s evaluations across the six tasks and two proposals per task. Third, attribute wording was held constant across profiles, pretested on-site during the Baku pilot, and kept neutral to reduce framing bias.

By design, however, a forced-choice conjoint captures relative preferences rather than absolute endorsement. Respondents may support some components of a proposal but still be required to choose between two imperfect bundles. Package-level choices therefore capture the net balance of respondents’ preferences across attributes, rather than standalone approval of any single reform. This is also what makes the design well suited to our research question. It reveals trade-off preferences that open-ended or Likert-scale items tend to obscure26,33. At the same time, it means that the estimates should be interpreted as the relative effect of replacing a baseline option with a given reform option within a proposal, not as a referendum on that reform in isolation.

The external validity of the findings is bounded by the composition of our elite sample. Although geographically diverse, the sample includes a relatively large share of Europe-based respondents among non-state actors and cannot be treated as statistically representative of all COP participants. Future work could extend this design in two directions: first, by repeating the experiment across successive COPs to assess whether preferences remain stable over time; and second, by combining conjoint estimates with follow-up interviews or text analysis of negotiation statements to compare stated preferences with revealed behaviour inside the negotiations.

Following consultation with Stockholm University, the study was determined not to require formal ethical review under applicable regulations (reference number SU FV-2123-26). The research design and survey administration were guided by established ethical standards for social science research involving human participants. Specifically, we prioritized respondent anonymity and voluntary participation throughout the study process. First, all participants were provided with detailed information about the study’s purpose and procedures and were required to give their informed consent before beginning the survey. Second, the survey was distributed via a fully anonymous link, ensuring that participation could not be traced back to individual respondents by the researchers or any third party. Third, to further safeguard confidentiality and minimize any risk of identification, the survey did not collect information regarding respondents’ country of origin, specific organizational role or title, or any sensitive political opinions or affiliations. No IP addresses or identifying metadata were recorded at any point. In addition, the survey was distributed via a fully anonymous link, ensuring that participation could not be traced back to individual respondents. Yet, some reforms within the UNFCCC do not depend on consensus but are in the hands of the political leadership of the Executive Secretary and the Presidency12. For instance, COP30 was named the COP of Implementation by the Brazilian Presidency, who sought to shape the Global Action Agenda to accelerate implementation. The COP30 outcome also included the Global Implementation Accelerator as a voluntary initiative led by the COP Presidencies. This demonstrates that agency of key actors can drive change when there is some demand for new initiatives.

Second, the results highlight which reforms are more contested. Limited support for changes to the COP presidency or representation rules suggests that these proposals would require substantial coalition-building to advance. Notably, changing the consensus rule does not emerge as a priority among respondents, in contrast to its prominence in much of the literature—an observation consistent with qualitative research on UNFCCC reform12. By identifying where support is strongest and weakest, the findings clarify which reform pathways are most likely to gain traction within the UNFCCC process.

Resistance to these reforms is not surprising. Presidency rotation reflects the UN’s regional-group balance; participation rules implicate states’ authority over accreditation; and consensus decision-making is widely seen by Parties as safeguarding sovereign equality6,30. Reforming these arrangements therefore carries higher political costs. Any such contested reforms should be pursued with caution, so as not to distract from the more feasible transparency and implementation agenda, where state and non-state actors show broader agreement.
